events.description: Al-Qaeda based in Sudan, investing in infrastructure (roads, schools); formally 'expelled' around 1996 though cells remained
Plot ordered by bin Laden: Abu Huzaifa fired a SAM at Prince Sultan Air Base; it failed to detonate and no one was hurt
Abu Huzaifa arrested in Sudan and extradited to Saudi Arabia in mid-2002; later released under murky circumstances
Bin Laden and Zawahiri each released a video calling for jihad in Darfur; bin Laden offered fighters from Iraq, rebuffed by Darfur rebels
Abu Huzaifa took part in a bomb plot just outside Khartoum; two more AQ leader videos on Sudan released
A U.S. diplomat and his driver were murdered in Sudan; claimed by Ansar al-Tahrid and AQ in the Land of Two Niles
actors: al-Qaeda in the Land of Two Niles

events.description: Another al-Qaeda video calling for jihad in Sudan
Abu Huzaifa took part in Zawahiri-ordered al-Qaeda reconciliation efforts among Syrian jihadists, co-signing statements with al-Maqdisi and Abu Qatada
U.S. raid on an al-Qaeda camp in Burmal district, Paktika killed Abu Khalil al-Sudani; intelligence found led to the Shorabak camps
Several months after the Paktika raid, U.S. and Afghan forces raided two large AQ training camps in Shorabak, killing 150-200 fighters
AQAP released Abu Huzaifa's book, a collection of letters to Sudanese mujahideen
Al-Maqdisi said Abu Huzaifa was arrested in Sudan after the book's release; Sudanese papers allude to it; unconfirmed
US raid on an al-Qaeda camp in Barmal district, Paktika, killed Abu Khalil al-Sudani; documents found revealed two large training camps in Shorabak, Kandahar.
Several months after the Paktika raid, US and Afghan forces raided the Shorabak camps and killed 150-200 al-Qaeda fighters.
Omar al-Bashir's dictatorship was deposed in Sudan; Abdalla Hamdok led the new government.
Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan overthrew Hamdok in a coup, creating a military junta.
Zawahiri issued the General Guidelines for Jihad, limiting targets to military, security and political ones and barring direct targeting of civilians.
Al-Shabaab attack in Somalia killed 100+ civilians 'just a couple days ago'; the group justified it by claiming the education ministry recruited fighters against them.
Abu Huzaifah al-Sudani published an 83-page manual for starting jihad in Sudan.
Death of Osama bin Laden, after which Zawahiri issued guidelines to put his stamp on al-Qaeda.
Sudani's long jihadist pedigree reportedly begins in the mid-90s, alongside bin Laden in Afghanistan.
Sudani reportedly performed a terrorist attack in Saudi Arabia in early 2001.
Al-Qaeda conducted internal evaluations ('fitness reports') of members, some of whom later joined the general manager's staff.
An AQ cell based in Salama, a suburb of Khartoum, carried out a bombing. Sudanese authorities quickly rolled it up. Sudani says it failed by applying the Iraqi model too early.

An AQ cell in Dinder National Park attacked a park guard post and captured a large cache of weapons. The Sudanese state then destroyed the cell. Sudani says it lacked vision, goals and cohesive leadership.
A Sudanese jihadist who had become an AQ commander in Mali, believed to have come from the Dinder camp, was killed.
AQAP published an earlier Sudani book on al-Qaeda in Mali (2018 or 2019), which drew lessons from 2012.
Zawahiri was killed, 21 years after 9/11.

key_claims: Abu Huzaifa al-Sudani's book is al-Qaeda's boilerplate playbook for building jihadist organizations (military wing, preaching, recruiting), applicable beyond Sudan.
Abu Huzaifa is a veteran al-Qaeda figure with ties to bin Laden, participation in a 2001 Saudi SAM plot, and co-signed statements with top ideologues such as al-Maqdisi and Abu Qatada.
The hosts argue al-Qaeda is a self-critical learning institution, and the book candidly admits al-Qaeda's failed startup cells in Khartoum and southern Sudan.
After its 1996 'expulsion' from Sudan, al-Qaeda left behind recruiters, financiers and operational leaders such as Abu Hassam and Abu Yahya al-Sudani, who sent recruits to Lashkar-e-Taiba.
Groups like Lashkar-e-Taiba and the Haqqanis relabel fighters across the Afghanistan-Pakistan border for plausible deniability, and LeT is tied to al-Qaeda's founding.

Al-Qaeda has failed to start a group in Sudan despite repeated calls from bin Laden and Zawahiri in 2006-2009, but has been successful at recruiting Sudanese for other theaters (Mali, Somalia, Yemen, Afghanistan).
The 2015 Paktika raid that killed Abu Khalil al-Sudani, sheltered in Haqqani territory, showed al-Qaeda's Afghan presence was far larger than U.S. intelligence's 50-100 fighters claim.
Abu Khalil al-Sudani was sheltered by the Haqqani Network in Paktika; documents from his death revealed the large al-Qaeda camps in Shorabak, Kandahar, undermining the 50-100 fighter narrative.

Abu Huzaifah's Sudan manual prescribes a dawa-first approach, a three-council structure, rural bases with urban cells, and an external operations wing, drawing on Maoist insurgency and the Taliban model.
Al-Qaeda's lessons from Mali and Yemen (Wuhayshi-Droukdel letters) inform the advice to avoid imposing harsh policies too quickly.

Ideologues and preachers such as Abu Huzaifah, Aboud Rogo, Awlaki and Maqdisi are portrayed as more dangerous than operational leaders because they recruit and provide religious justification, and their legacy outlives them.
Zawahiri's 2013 General Guidelines bar direct targeting of civilians but allow economic targets, and groups like al-Shabaab regularly rationalize civilian deaths.
Sudanese al-Qaeda veterans appear across branches (Shabaab, AQEA, AQAP, Hurras al-Din, Afghanistan), yet al-Qaeda has historically failed to build a group inside Sudan.
Sudani's book analyses two failed AQ efforts in Sudan, the 2007 Salama cell and the 2012 Dinder National Park cell, and gives insider detail that suggests he was linked to them.
Sudani argues that jihad in Sudan must be built from the ground up through recruiting, proselytizing and networks, and that the Iraqi model cannot be imposed without the right conditions.
Sudani endorses economic targeting, including of Sudan's economy, in line with al-Qaeda's long-standing practice.
The hosts judge AQ more dangerous than IS because it learns from its mistakes and plays the long game, while IS jihadists seek immediate gratification.

The hosts say the Dinder cell was al-Qaeda, as Sudani's account now confirms. It trained fighters for Mali and Somalia, and a Sudanese AQ commander killed in Mali in 2013 is believed to have come from that camp.
The hosts see Sudani as an under-recognised core al-Qaeda leader who rose to prominence, likely has deputies, and is a sign that killing legacy leaders will not end the group.

Hibatullah Akhundzada is an ideological leader rather than a military one, and the Taliban's victory rested on recruitment and indoctrination on both sides of the border, including pulling in al-Qaeda members.
